and for ecom google ads, the economics of creative production change entirely. here's the exact prompt framework we run

the shopping image prompt:

"generate a premium ecommerce product image of [product description]. product on the right third against a [lifestyle setting: marble surface / wooden table / kitchen counter]. dramatic rim lighting from the upper left. clean contact shadow. realistic material texture. no text overlay. no watermark. aspect ratio 1:1"

why lifestyle over product-on-white: 9 out of 10 shopping listings use product-on-white, so the listing with a lifestyle image breaks the pattern and pulls 2-3x higher CTR because the buyer's eye locks onto the visual outlier in the grid

for the jewelry brand we scaled to 8-figure months, the winning shopping image was an unboxing reaction shot instead of a necklace on a white background. a woman opening the box with her hands over her mouth. the emotional resonance of one image outperformed every studio product shot they'd tested

the text-overlay ad prompt:

"generate a high-impact static ad in 4:5 portrait (1024x1280). [product] in lifestyle setting. overlay text in bold sans-serif: headline '[pain-point phrase from buyer research]' at the top. subtext '[mechanism or benefit]' below. CTA button '[action text]' at the bottom in [brand colour]. clean layout with negative space"

previous AI image models rendered text looking blurry and misspelled. GPT images 2.0 renders text pixel-perfect. your static ads have readable headlines, pricing, and CTAs baked directly into the image with no photoshop and no designer, all from one prompt

the before/after prompt:

"generate a split-frame image. left side: [person experiencing the problem, frustrated expression, muted colours]. right side: same person experiencing the outcome, happy expression, warm colours]. dividing line down the centre. no text overlay. 16:9 for display ads"

before/after imagery converts across every niche. the visual contrast compresses the entire advertorial narrative into one image

the production math:

traditional product photography runs $2-5k per session on a two-week timeline

GPT images 2.0 runs $0.05-0.21 per image with three-second generation time

10-50x cheaper, 1,000x faster, and every image is grounded in buyer psychology from the ICP research rather than the creative director's gut feeling

the brands running AI-generated shopping images alongside AI-generated youtube shorts are producing 10x the creative volume at 10% of the cost, and the hit rate is higher because every creative is built from real buyer language

🇬🇧 LONDON BOOKSHOP ACCUSED OF GIVING HITLER’S MEIN KAMPF “DANGEROUS NEW POWER”

Aafaq Bookstore on London’s Edgware Road has been found selling Arabic-language copies of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf, reportedly displayed with a photograph of Hitler giving the Nazi salute.

The book’s ideological importance is beyond dispute: Mein Kampf laid out central elements of Hitler’s National Socialist worldview and foreshadowed the genocidal policies and wars that followed. More than 12 million copies were sold before the fall of Nazi Germany.

The issue, argues writer Robin Schäfer, is not simply whether the book is available—but how it is presented and contextualized.

Schäfer writes:

“There is a difference between preserving a poisonous historical text and peddling it.”

He points to Germany’s Institute for Contemporary History (IfZ), which produced a critical edition with more than 3,500 scholarly annotations designed to expose Hitler’s distortions and place his claims against historical research.

Schäfer argues:

“Availability is not the same as endorsement.”

But he warns that an unannotated translation, particularly one marketed with Hitler’s image in a Nazi salute, can strip away the historical context and potentially turn the text into a vehicle for modern propaganda.

“There is no scholarly reason to reproduce Hitler’s image in mid-salute.”

And his conclusion is blunt:

“It is imperative to deconstruct Hitler and his propaganda thoroughly, thereby depriving this dangerous book of its symbolic power. Aafaq Bookstore has done the opposite.”

The debate is not about banning history. It is about whether a text responsible for helping articulate a genocidal ideology should be presented as serious historical material—or marketed with the very imagery that helped create its cultic power.

Mein Kampf in Arabic is precisely what they teach in the Muslim countries, and this is why it’s now the Islamic Republic of Britain.

Via: Mossad National Intel Desk

The emergence of procedural world generation from textual prompts, as demonstrated in applications rendering narrative environments from literary sources, highlights a significant threshold in generative modeling. This capability moves beyond static image or text creation into the synthesis of dynamic, interactive systems. Karpathy's observation of a large language model orchestrating polygonal assets in 3D space from a high-level description aligns with research in grounded language acquisition, where symbolic representations must be mapped to sensory or simulated environments.

This process can be framed within the context of "program synthesis," a field that has seen substantial progress with models like AlphaCode. However, the task here is complex, involving the translation of abstract narrative concepts ("a party of special magnificence") into concrete spatial and temporal arrangements. The "jank" or error in the output, as noted, underscores the grounding problem: the model's capacity to generate syntactically correct code for a renderer exists alongside a limited ability to "perceive" or internally validate the resulting visual-kinematic experience.

This limitation points to a core area of research in embodied AI. Work by researchers like Jitendra Malik and colleagues on learning from video and interaction suggests that models require feedback loops that are more integrated than textual or static image-based supervision. An LLM's inability to "play the game" it has created is analogous to a lack of proprioceptive or visual feedback, a challenge that work in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and simulation-to-real transfer attempts to address. The potential for "ephemeral GTA of X on demand" is contingent on solving this validation and iteration cycle, likely through multimodal architectures that can process video or interactive state data as natively as they process text.

I’ve been using @sleepagotchi for a while, and what keeps me interested is how much the product has evolved.

It started with the sleep to earn idea, but it feels like they’re building something much broader now.

Instead of opening an app, checking a sleep score, looking at a few charts, and moving on, the AI Sleep Coach actually gives you some context around your night. It points out changes, explains what might have caused them, and gives you a couple of practical things to try.

That part feels far more useful to me than the usual “sleep more” advice.

What I find even more interesting is how the different coaches are starting to connect. Sleep data can lead into conversations around energy, stress, daily habits, food, and recovery. The Meal Planner and Shopping Agent are still being rolled out, but you can already see where the product is heading.

The privacy side is also worth mentioning. Your biometric data stays on your phone, while anything processed externally is anonymized and not retained. That matters when you’re dealing with something as personal as health and recovery data.

Personally, I’ve noticed small changes. I’m more deliberate about when I go to bed, I pay more attention to recovery instead of just counting hours, and the feedback makes it easier to stay consistent.

And yes, 2.2 million users is impressive.

But I think the bigger story is whether people keep opening the app every day because it genuinely helps them. That kind of retention says far more than points, rewards, or a virtual pet ever could.

I still don't understand why nobody talks about what NVIDIA's GPU clusters are actually being used for beyond chatbots and image generation.

Pharmaceutical companies are simulating billions of drug compounds on H100s. Protein folding calculations that took years in a lab now run in weeks. Molecular interactions that required physical experiments are being screened computationally at a scale no research team could match manually.

NVIDIA calls these AI factories. Not data centers. Factories. Because the output isn't compute time or generated text.

It's drug candidates that go directly into clinical pipelines.

The same chip powering your AI assistant is quietly running simulations that could produce the next cancer treatment. Same hardware. Completely different stakes.

Most people have no idea this is happening. That's the part worth paying attention to.
